lines.text: regard to ourselves; it deprives us of the power of self-criti-
cism. In our text we read:
"Why should a living man complain,
a man, about the punishment of his sins?" (3: 39.)
Or more precisely translated:
"What has a living man the right to complain of?
It is his sin that each one should lament!"
What then is the ultimate source of the distress and suffering
in which we are involved? Is it ultimately the fault of the
conquerors that so many of us are without homes and shelter?
Are they responsible for the fact that we go hungry? We
do not propose in this place to discuss in all its breadth and
scope the vexed question of guilt. It is certain, however, that
not every one of us is guilty to the same degree, and that
there are many innocent people who have been swept into
this tide of bitter pain and suffering for which they are in
no wise responsible. It is also certain that the question of
guilt bears differently on German youth than on the older
generation; for the latter the situation is much more op-
pressive because on them lies the responsibility for youth,
and for the young our common distress is much more
terrible than for us older people.
It is not our business here to discuss in general terms the
question of guilt in so far as this is a political question, a
question to be treated as between human beings. There is
only one thing we have to say on the point here and now:
it is that only patience and inner calm of mind can and
should render possible an objective consideration of the
matter. We shall never come to an understanding with each
other if bitterness and passion prevail. Having said that, we
must add: we stand before the sight of God, and in the eyes
of the Most Holy no one of us is pure. Everyone is in some
way a participant and somehow responsible when in our
nation things are not as they should be. And if in our suffer-
ing we cry out and complain with embittered and indignant
hearts, then we should heed those words which we do not
like to hear:
